talks.title: The SEPodcast Ep 120 Live Guest Robin Dreeke
talks.teaser: Live podcast episode featuring Robin Dreeke discussing rapport building, behavioral analysis, and defensive social engineering strategies.
talks.summary:
In this live episode of The Social-Engineer Podcast (Ep. 120) recorded at the DEF CON 27 Social Engineering Village, host Chris Hadnagy welcomes guest Robin Dreeke, former head of the FBI's Counterintelligence Behavioral Analysis Program, to celebrate the village's tenth anniversary. At 12:00, Robin breaks down the psychological principles of non-verbal communication, positive social indicators, and interpersonal rapport building, explaining how authentic curiosity and non-judgmental validation disarm human suspicion.

The conversation transitions to operational vishing tactics at 24:00, where Robin and Chris discuss handling immediate hang-ups, dialing rhythm, and the subtle linguistic cues that convince call recipients to cooperate. At 36:00, they reflect on the decade-long evolution of the SE Village, highlighting how social engineering transformed from an overlooked novelty into a recognized discipline within cybersecurity.

Robin offers pragmatic career guidance at 48:00, advising job seekers on how to bypass automated applicant tracking systems by initiating direct human conversations with hiring managers and industry mentors. At 01:00:00, they examine high-volume vishing engagements, analyzing how enterprise teams handle dozens of pretext calls per hour during compliance assessments. They close at 01:12:00 with gratitude for the global social engineering community and the enduring value of human-centered security defense. (AI summary — Gemini Flash)

talks.title: OSINT in the Real World
talks.teaser: Practical OSINT techniques applicable to security careers and daily life—real investigation walkthroughs and personal case studies.
talks.summary:
Ryan MacDougall, an experienced social engineer and OSINT practitioner, illustrates how open-source intelligence methodologies can be applied beyond traditional information security engagements to address practical problems and enhance personal safety in daily life.

[05:40] MacDougall presents real-world investigative case studies, demonstrating how public records and online telemetry can be used to vet home improvement contractors [11:18], assess Craigslist transactions, investigate neighborhood safety and zoning history when purchasing real estate, and verify prospective dates or roommates.

[16:52] The talk walks through practical research workflows, showing how to cross-reference municipal property records, tax assessor databases, court registries, and social media footprints to corroborate background stories and uncover concealed liabilities. MacDougall discusses passive reconnaissance techniques [23:13], operational security (OPSEC) for personal researchers, and the importance of adhering to strict ethical and legal boundaries to ensure OSINT investigations do not cross into harassment or invasion of privacy.

talks.title: Red Teaming Insights and Examples from Beyond
talks.teaser: Red team approaches beyond penetration testing—how military, intelligence, and private sector organizations use red teaming for strategic defense.
talks.summary:
In this talk at the DEF CON 27 Social Engineering Village, foreign policy expert and author Micah Zenko ("Red Team: How to Succeed by Thinking Like the Enemy") discusses applying red teaming methodologies beyond information technology into institutional and strategic decision-making. He opens at 05:00 by analyzing the severe impact of cognitive biases on high-stakes executive decisions, demonstrating how confirmation bias and groupthink routinely lead leadership to catastrophic policy failures.

Micah explains at 10:00 why conventional organizations struggle to capture contrarian insights, noting that institutional hierarchies naturally incentivize conformity and suppress dissenting viewpoints. To counter this, he outlines structured methodologies for designing red team exercises, tabletop simulations, and alternative analysis games at 15:00, emphasizing that simulations must test actual operational procedures under realistic failure conditions.

At 20:00, Micah issues a strong warning regarding executive buy-in: commissioning a red team only to ignore or dismiss its uncomfortable conclusions is more damaging than conducting no assessment at all, as it signals that candor is penalized. He wraps up at 25:00 by examining flawed social science around brainstorming and advocating for rigorous, independent red teams empowered to challenge fundamental institutional assumptions. (AI summary — Gemini Flash)

talks.title: The Aspies Guide to Social Engineering
talks.teaser: Neurodivergent perspectives on social engineering—how autism and different thinking styles bring unique strengths to security defense.
talks.summary:
Perry Carpenter delivers an insightful and introspective presentation exploring the intersection of neurodiversity and human hacking in "The Aspies Guide to Social Engineering," examining how an autistic cognitive profile can be applied to master social engineering.

[06:36] Sharing his personal diagnosis on the autism spectrum (Asperger's syndrome), Carpenter explains how the unique traits of autistic thinking—such as hyper-systematization, intense pattern recognition, and an analytical view of social rules—allow practitioners to view human interactions through a structured, programmatic lens.

[12:57] Because intuitive social rapport does not occur naturally for individuals on the spectrum, Carpenter describes the process of building explicit cognitive algorithms to decode human behavior. He explains how analyzing conversational scripts, body language, pacing, and simulated empathy [19:02] can lead to profound insights into human decision heuristics. The talk concludes by connecting these behavioral mechanisms to enterprise security [25:24], showing how an understanding of cognitive dissonance, cognitive load, and human biases can inform the design of more empathetic and effective security awareness initiatives.

talks.title: Swing Away  Conquer Impostor Syndrome
talks.teaser: Overcoming impostor syndrome—psychological barriers affecting security professionals and how to break through self-doubt cycles.
talks.summary:
In this engaging and personal session at the DEF CON 27 Social Engineering Village, Billy Boatright addresses the pervasive challenge of impostor syndrome across the infosec and hacker community. Drawing from his childhood experiences playing Little League baseball at 04:00, Billy illustrates how early fears of striking out mirror the professional anxiety of being exposed as unqualified or out of place.

Billy relates this struggle to competitive theater auditions at 08:00, describing the intimidation of performing alongside world-champion jugglers and seasoned professionals. At 12:00, he deconstructs "hero worship" within the cybersecurity industry, analyzing how putting prominent keynote speakers on pedestals fosters unrealistic expectations and deepens self-doubt among practitioners.

At 16:00, Billy urges attendees to view industry role models not as infallible icons, but as peers whose dedication can serve as inspiration rather than intimidation. He encourages the audience at 20:00 to overcome hesitation, submit to CFPs, and step up to the plate ("swing away"), asserting that everyone brings a valuable perspective to the security discipline regardless of tenure. He concludes at 24:00 with an open Q&A on managing anxiety, accepting vulnerability, and mentoring newcomers. (AI summary — Gemini Flash)

talks.title: SEVillage 10 Year Anniversary a Look Back
talks.teaser: Retrospective on 10 years of Social Engineering Village—evolution from underground gatherings to mainstream security awareness.
talks.summary:
Chris Hadnagy commemorates the tenth anniversary of the Social Engineering Village (SE Village), looking back at its origins, high-profile controversies, community growth, and its lasting impact on information security culture.

[10:14] Hadnagy recounts the village's launch at DEF CON 18 in 2010, recalling the initial skepticism and intense mainstream media storm sparked by the live, soundproof vishing booth competitions. He reflects on how demonstrations of phone-based elicitation exposed severe vulnerabilities in corporate defense models, sharing memorable moments including an impromptu visit by NSA Director General Keith Alexander [12:43].

[25:39] The presentation highlights the maturation of the Social Engineering Capture the Flag (SECTF) competition, the creation of educational initiatives like SECTF for Kids, and the careers launched within the village. Hadnagy underscores the guiding philosophy of the SE Village—to "leave people better than you found them" [37:47]—emphasizing that ethical social engineering must prioritize education, empathy, and positive reinforcement over mockery. He concludes by analyzing modern social engineering trends, automated phishing, and the continuous need for human-centric defense training.

talks.title: The Voice Told Me To Do It
talks.teaser: Voice-based social engineering—leveraging authority and psychological pressure to manipulate victims into compliance.
talks.summary:
In this dynamic presentation at the DEF CON 27 Social Engineering Village, Daniel Isler combines his background as a professional actor, university professor, and security consultant to explore how vocal technique and psychological persuasion influence human behavior. He introduces the role of vocal archetypes at 04:00, discussing how adjusting pitch, tone, resonance, and tempo can instantly establish authority, portray vulnerability, or diffuse suspicion during physical and social engineering engagements.

At 08:00, Daniel emphasizes the necessity of spontaneity and active listening, demonstrating that rigid scripts fail when human targets deviate from expected reactions. He shares personal stories of mentorship and artistic training at 12:00, illustrating how mastering emotional delivery allows social engineers to project genuine authenticity.

Daniel recounts physical penetration testing engagements across Chile and South America at 16:00, walking through how vocal calibration enabled him to talk his way past security checkpoints and private security personnel. At 20:00, he shares an audio demonstration illustrating how cadence and assertiveness guided security guards into compliant behavior. He concludes at 24:00 with an audience discussion on the ethical application of vocal persuasion techniques in adversary simulation. (AI summary — Gemini Flash)

talks.title: Rideshare OSINT Car-Based SE For Fun and Profit
talks.teaser: OSINT and social engineering via rideshare interactions—gathering intelligence and testing security through Uber and Lyft engagements.
talks.summary:
Edward Miro discusses the unique intersection of rideshare driving and social engineering, illustrating how working as an Uber or Lyft driver serves as an exceptional training environment for honing elicitation techniques, cold reading, and collecting open-source intelligence (OSINT).

[06:32] Miro explains that the confined, semi-private atmosphere of a vehicle ride naturally lowers passenger inhibitions, creating an ideal setting for developing social engineering skills. He discusses the fundamentals of cold reading, active listening, and matching a passenger's mood and tone [17:01] to establish immediate rapport and trust.

[20:56] The talk highlights significant operational security (OPSEC) vulnerabilities observed during rideshare trips. Miro recounts how business travelers, corporate executives, and technical staff frequently discuss non-public corporate initiatives, merger activities, trade secrets, and internal organizational conflicts on speakerphone or with the driver. He stresses the critical need for employee awareness regarding physical and environmental eavesdropping, concluding with ethical considerations and guidelines for practicing interpersonal elicitation responsibly.
